title: Effect of martensite-austenite island decomposition during two-step tempering on the fracture surface morphology of impact and tensile tested Mn-Ni-Mo steel
abstract: Mn-Ni-Mo steels used in reactor pressure vessel manufacturing often exhibit martensite-austenite (M/A) islands post-quenching. These islands demonstrate the deleterious impact of M/A island decomposition on the mechanical properties of Mn-Ni-Mo steels, as they can decompose into long, rod-shaped Fe3C carbides when tempered above 600 °C. To address this issue, the current study investigates a two-step tempering process to gain deeper insight into the characteristics of M/A island decomposition and its impact on the mechanical properties and fracture surface morphology of tensile and impact-tested samples. The process involves a two-hour pre-tempering treatment at 200 °C, 350 °C, and 500 °C, followed by three hours of final tempering at 650 °C. The study reveals temperature-dependent characteristics of M/A island decomposition, as well as the significant impact of tempered microstructure and carbide precipitates (rod-shaped M3C, rhombus-shaped M7C3, and globular-shaped M23C6) on mechanical properties and fracture surface morphology. At 200 °C, the M/A island partially decomposes, resulting in long rod-shaped carbide precipitates during final tempering. These precipitates reduce the critical cleavage stress required for microcrack initiation, resulting in lower ultimate tensile strength and impact toughness. Furthermore, the fracture surface of the sample pre-tempered at 200 °C exhibits a higher percentage of cleavage facets than samples pre-tempered at 350 °C and 500 °C. Meanwhile, at 350 °C, the pre-tempering sample showed aggregated carbide precipitates of various sizes at former M/A island locations, resulting in the formation of numerous micro-voids in close proximity during the fracture. These voids eventually coalesce, forming a substantial crack that leads to material failure. The 500 °C pre-tempering sample contained coarse spherical carbides, and carbide precipitate clustering had disappeared. Samples pre-tempered at 300 °C and 500 °C had a higher fraction of ductile dimples, indicating better tensile properties. However, splitting-related decohesion and dimple depth increased as the pre-tempering temperature increased. All tempered samples show dimples and quasi-cleavage facets in the fracture propagation region, indicating a mixed-mode fracture mechanism.
